title: Race Condition
description: Race Condition is the 2001 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of nu-metal about doing many things at once, on one machine or many, plus a hidden thirteenth. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays downtuned seven-string guitar, Wyrd trades the keytar for turntables and samples, and Bytes plays drums and raps the backing vocals. Multicore processors, threads and shared memory, locks, barriers, message passing, embarrassingly parallel work, Amdahl’s law, logical clocks, partial failure, consensus and the CAP theorem. Recorded with all four members playing at once in separate rooms, so the title track came out two different ways. They released both. Play loud. Synchronize.
tagline: The 2001 nu-metal album from Procedural Byts: a parallel and distributed computing course in twelve songs, plus a hidden thirteenth.
lineup: The four-piece, running in parallel. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays downtuned seven-string guitar. Wyrd plays turntables and samples. Bytes plays drums and raps the backing vocals.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the version of the title track that resolves. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass, and on this album she shares the microphone the way you share a lock.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, three more strings than the 1980s, and still no guitar solos. Qword responded by recording the same riff four times and playing all four at once.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, and as of 2001 a DJ. Wyrd scratches two copies of the same record against each other on the title track and lets them race.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, and the band’s new rapper. Bytes plays drums, raps every bridge on the album, and his tape machine starting first is why the hidden track exists.

members.name: Null
members.bio: The fifth vote. Abstains every time. Has never lost an election.

story.heading: Two Versions
paragraphs: The new millennium arrived, and with it, nu-metal. Wyrd traded the keytar for a pair of turntables. Qword got a seven-string guitar and was told, again, that guitar solos would not be happening this decade. Bytes discovered he could rap, and nobody has been able to stop him since.
To save studio time, the producer had all four members record at the same moment, in four separate rooms, with no click track and no way to hear each other. Four threads, one shared tape.

It mostly worked. But the title track came out differently depending on whose tape machine started first. When Nyble’s started first, the song resolved. When Bytes’s started first, the chorus came in a bar early and the whole thing collapsed into a crash. The band couldn’t agree which version was the real one, so they released both. The second one is hidden at the end of the album.

On tour, the band traveled in two buses. A snowstorm cut the phone lines between them for two days, and each bus assumed the other had crashed. Neither had. Each bus decided the setlist on its own, and both ended up playing the same city on the same night, at different venues. The band calls it the split-brain tour.
After that, every decision went to a vote. With four members, every vote tied two to two, so they started counting Null as a fifth voter. The duck abstains every time, and somehow that settles it.

cover_sub: The 2001 album. Four members, four rooms, no click track, two versions of the title track.

songs.title: Race Condition (Nyble First)

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Two of us reach for the same thing at the same time,
I read it, you read it, and we both think it’s fine.
I write it, you write it, and one of us is lost,
Whoever gets there last decides, and nobody counts the cost!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Race condition! (Who got there first?)
Race condition! (Better or worse?)
Same code, different timing, a different song each night,
Race condition, race condition, and nothing comes out right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It works on my machine, it works a thousand times,
Then once a week it fails and leaves no trace behind.
It hides when you go looking, it shows up when you’re gone,
The timing is the bug, and it’s been there all along!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Check, then act! You checked, it changed!
Read, modify, write, and the value’s rearranged!
Two threads, one variable, and nobody in charge,
Make it atomic, or the damage gets large!

parts.label: Turntable solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays two copies of the same record on two turntables at once and lets them race. In this version, the left record wins by half a beat, and the song resolves.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Race condition! (Who got there first?)
Race condition! (Better or worse?)
Same code, different timing, a different song each night,
Race condition, race condition, and nothing comes out right!

songs.note: Version one of two. In this version, Nyble’s tape machine started first and the song resolves. The other version is hidden at the end of the album.
songs.lesson: A race condition happens when a program’s result depends on the timing of things running at the same time. Two threads read the same value, both add one and both write it back, and one update is lost; or a thread checks something and it changes before it acts. Race conditions are intermittent and hard to reproduce: same program, same input, different result. The fix is to make the operation atomic or to synchronize access.

songs.title: Many Cores

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: One core switching quickly makes it look like all at once,
That’s concurrency, it’s juggling, one ball at a time it runs.
Put four cores on the chip and now they really run together,
That’s parallel, four hands at once, in any kind of weather!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Many cores! (Running side by side!)
Many cores! (Nowhere left to hide!)
The clock stopped getting faster, so we built it wide instead,
Many cores, many cores, and a thread for every head!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The heat got way too high when we pushed the clock up more,
So the chips stopped getting faster and they started getting four.
Now every program has to learn to split itself in parts,
Or three of the four cores sit and wait with idle hearts!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Concurrent! Taking turns on a single core!
Parallel! Doing four at once, and more!

parts.label: Riff breakdown: Qword
parts.desc: Qword was told there would be no guitar solos this decade either, so Qword recorded the same riff four times and played all four at once, one for each core. It is the heaviest thing on the album.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Many cores! (Running side by side!)
Many cores! (Nowhere left to hide!)
The clock stopped getting faster, so we built it wide instead,
Many cores, many cores, and a thread for every head!

songs.note: The first multicore processor shipped in 2001. The band bought a machine with two and named each core after a member. Wyrd and Bytes are still arguing about who got left out.
songs.lesson: Concurrency means structuring a program as several tasks that can make progress independently, even if one core is taking turns between them. Parallelism means actually running them at the same moment on several cores. Around 2001 to 2005, heat and power limits ended the race for faster clock speeds, so chips started adding cores instead, and software has to run in parallel to get faster.

songs.title: Shared Memory

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: We all live in the same house and we all can read the walls,
Every thread can see the memory, every thread can make the calls.
Fast to share, no need to send, just write it and it’s there,
But when two of us write the same spot, nobody knows who’s where!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Shared memory! (Everybody sees!)
Shared memory! (Everybody writes!)
Easy to share and easy to break in the middle of the night,
Shared memory, shared memory, and nobody’s right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A thread is a path through the program with its own stack and place,
But the heap is common ground, a crowded open space.
Every core has its own cache with a copy of the view,
And keeping all the copies honest is the hardest thing to do!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Thread one! Thread two! Same address space!
Cache one! Cache two! Who’s got the latest case?

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble starts a slap-bass phrase, and halfway through Wyrd’s sampler overwrites the end of it with a different one, because they were both writing to the same bar.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Shared memory! (Everybody sees!)
Shared memory! (Everybody writes!)
Easy to share and easy to break in the middle of the night,
Shared memory, shared memory, and nobody’s right!

songs.note: Nyble and Wyrd both recorded into the same bar of tape on this song. Neither knew the other was doing it.
songs.lesson: Threads in the same process share memory, like the heap and global variables, while each thread has its own stack. Sharing makes communication fast, but writes that aren’t synchronized can collide. Each core also keeps its own cache, and hardware cache coherence keeps those copies consistent; making sure one thread sees another’s writes still needs synchronization.

songs.title: Mutex

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Only one microphone and four of us to sing,
Grab it, hold it, sing your part, and then give up the thing.
That’s a mutex, only one inside the room,
Everybody else waits outside in the gloom!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Mutex! (Lock it!)
Mutex! (Unlock it!)
One at a time in the critical section, the rest wait in line,
Mutex, mutex, and the data’s fine!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Hold the lock too long and the others sit and stare,
Lock too little and the race is waiting there.
Atomic operations, one step that can’t be split,
Compare and swap in one move, and no one interrupts it!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Acquire! (I’m in!) Release! (You’re next!)
Forget to release and the whole thing’s wrecked!
Lock two things in different orders and the deadlock’s back,
Always lock in the same order and you’re on the right track!

parts.label: Drum breakdown: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a breakdown where only one drum is allowed to sound at a time. He passes the beat from snare to kick to tom like a lock, and when he tries to hit two at once, he stops himself.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Mutex! (Lock it!)
Mutex! (Unlock it!)
One at a time in the critical section, the rest wait in line,
Mutex, mutex, and the data’s fine!

songs.note: The rap verse was supposed to be Bytes’s alone. Nyble kept stepping on it until they agreed to pass the microphone like a lock.
songs.lesson: A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) lets only one thread at a time into a critical section. Hold locks briefly so the other threads aren’t stuck waiting, always release them, and take multiple locks in the same order everywhere to avoid deadlock. Atomic instructions like compare-and-swap update a value in one indivisible step, and they’re the building block underneath locks.

songs.title: Barrier

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Everyone works on their own piece of the job,
Some of us are quick and some of us are slow.
But nobody moves to the next phase till everybody’s done,
The barrier holds us here until the last one’s come!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Barrier! (Wait for me!)
Barrier! (Wait for all!)
Nobody crosses the line till the last one hears the call,
Barrier, barrier, and then we move as one!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Phase one, compute, phase two, exchange,
Phase three, compute again, and the pattern doesn’t change.
The fastest thread is waiting on the slowest every time,
So balance out the load, or the waiting is a crime!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: One’s here! Two’s here! Three’s here! Where’s four?
Four’s here! Now we go! Break down the door!

parts.label: Staggered fills: full band
parts.desc: Each member plays a fill of a different length. Nyble finishes first and waits, then Qword, then Wyrd. Bytes finishes last, and only then does the whole band slam into the chorus together.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Barrier! (Wait for me!)
Barrier! (Wait for all!)
Nobody crosses the line till the last one hears the call,
Barrier, barrier, and then we move as one!

songs.note: Every chorus on this song waits until all four members have arrived, even if someone gets there early.
songs.lesson: A barrier is a synchronization point: every thread stops there and waits until all of them have arrived, then they all continue. It’s common in algorithms that work in phases. Because each phase lasts as long as the slowest thread, load balancing, giving every thread a similar amount of work, matters a lot.

songs.title: Message Passing

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: No shared house this time, we each live on our own,
Every process has its memory, every process is alone.
If I want you to know something, I have to send it through,
A message on the wire from me straight to you!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Message passing! (Send it!)
Message passing! (Receive it!)
Nothing shared and nothing broken, every copy is our own,
Message passing, message passing, and we’re never alone!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Send and receive, the receiver waits until it’s there,
Copy what you need, and there’s no memory to share.
It scales across a room of machines, a building or the sea,
A thousand processes talking, and not a lock to see!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Send! (To you!) Receive! (From me!)
No locks, no races, just messages, see?

parts.label: Call and answer: Nyble and Bytes
parts.desc: Nyble sends a phrase on the bass, and Bytes waits until he’s received all of it before sending his reply on the drums. They never play at the same time and never step on each other.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Message passing! (Send it!)
Message passing! (Receive it!)
Nothing shared and nothing broken, every copy is our own,
Message passing, message passing, and we’re never alone!

songs.note: Recorded with Nyble and Bytes in different cities, sending parts back and forth. They had done this before, in 1982.
songs.lesson: In message passing, processes don’t share memory at all. They communicate by sending and receiving messages, as in MPI, the standard from 1994. There are no shared-variable races, it scales across many machines, and every bit of communication is explicit, at the cost of copying data and waiting for messages to arrive.

songs.title: Embarrassingly Parallel

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A thousand photos and I need them all made small,
Each one on its own, they don’t depend on each other at all.
Give one to every worker and they never need to speak,
It’s so easy that it’s embarrassing, and done within the week!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Embarrassingly parallel! (No talking!)
Embarrassingly parallel! (No waiting!)
Split it up and hand it out and gather it at the end,
Embarrassingly parallel, the easy kind, my friend!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The same operation on every piece of data in the set,
Data parallel, the easiest win you’ll ever get.
Different tasks at the same time, that’s task parallel too,
Map it out to all the workers, then collect it back to you!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: One for you! One for you! One for you! One for me!
No locks! No messages! Speedup for free!

parts.label: Independent parts: full band
parts.desc: Each member recorded their part alone, without hearing anyone else, and the parts still fit perfectly, because none of them depends on the others.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Embarrassingly parallel! (No talking!)
Embarrassingly parallel! (No waiting!)
Split it up and hand it out and gather it at the end,
Embarrassingly parallel, the easy kind, my friend!

songs.note: The easiest song on the album to record: everyone played their part with no one else in the room, and it still fit.
songs.lesson: Embarrassingly parallel problems split into independent tasks that need little or no communication, like resizing thousands of photos or rendering separate frames of a film, so they speed up almost perfectly as you add processors. Data parallelism applies the same operation to many pieces of data at once; task parallelism runs different tasks at the same time.

[Verse 1: female lead vocal]
A thousand photos and I need them all made small,
Each one on its own, they don’t depend on each other at all.
Give one to every worker and they never need to speak,
It’s so easy that it’s embarrassing, and done within the week!

[Chorus: female lead vocal, male shouted backing vocals]
Embarrassingly parallel! (No talking!)
Embarrassingly parallel! (No waiting!)
Split it up and hand it out and gather it at the end,
Embarrassingly parallel, the easy kind, my friend!

[Verse 2: female lead vocal]
The same operation on every piece of data in the set,
Data parallel, the easiest win you’ll ever get.
Different tasks at the same time, that’s task parallel too,
Map it out to all the workers, then collect it back to you!

[Chorus: female lead vocal, male shouted backing vocals]
Embarrassingly parallel! (No talking!)
Embarrassingly parallel! (No waiting!)
Split it up and hand it out and gather it at the end,
Embarrassingly parallel, the easy kind, my friend!

[Bridge: male rap vocals]
One for you! One for you! One for you! One for me!
No locks! No messages! Speedup for free!

[Instrumental Break: four completely independent instrumental parts that fit together perfectly]

[Final Chorus: female lead vocal, male shouted backing vocals]
Embarrassingly parallel! (No talking!)
Embarrassingly parallel! (No waiting!)
Split it up and hand it out and gather it at the end,
Embarrassingly parallel, the easy kind, my friend!

[End]

songs.title: Amdahl

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Ten percent of the program has to run one step at a time,
Ninety percent can split across the cores, and that part’s fine.
Add a thousand cores and the ninety disappears,
But the ten percent is waiting, and it’s still here!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Amdahl’s law! (The serial part!)
Amdahl’s law! (Breaks your heart!)
Ten percent alone means ten times is the best you’ll see,
Amdahl’s law, Amdahl’s law, and the limit’s plain to see!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Speedup is the old time over new time on the clock,
But the part that won’t divide is the part you can’t unlock.
So grow the problem bigger, Gustafson came to say,
More cores for bigger jobs, and the serial part fades away!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Two cores! (Faster!) Eight cores! (Faster!)
A thousand cores! (Not much faster, master!)

parts.label: The serial part: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays one slow eight-bar phrase that only one instrument can play. Around it, the band speeds up and adds more and more parts, but the song can never finish faster than Wyrd’s eight bars.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Amdahl’s law! (The serial part!)
Amdahl’s law! (Breaks your heart!)
Ten percent alone means ten times is the best you’ll see,
Amdahl’s law, Amdahl’s law, and the limit’s plain to see!

songs.note: The intro is the same eight bars no matter how many musicians join in. That’s the point.
songs.lesson: Amdahl’s law: if a fraction of a program has to run one step at a time, that fraction limits the speedup no matter how many processors you add. With 10% serial, the best possible speedup is 10 times. Speedup is old time divided by new time. Gustafson’s law points out that with more processors we usually tackle bigger problems, so the parallel part grows and scaling looks much better.

songs.title: Lamport Clock

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Your clock says five, my clock says ten past,
Neither one is wrong, but neither one will last.
There’s no single clock that every machine can see,
So what came first, the message or the reply from me?

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Lamport clock! (Count the events!)
Lamport clock! (Make it make sense!)
If it caused it, it came before, and that’s all we need to know,
Lamport clock, Lamport clock, and the order’s set to go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Keep a counter, add one each time something happens here,
Send the counter with the message so the order’s clear.
When you receive, jump ahead past the number that you got,
Happened-before is all we have, and happened-before is a lot!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Sent it at three! Got it at four!
Can’t get a message before it’s sent, and that’s the law!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays two patterns at slightly different tempos on two halves of the kit, and they drift apart. Every time one sends a cue hit, the other jumps ahead to stay after it. They never agree on the time, only on the order.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Lamport clock! (Count the events!)
Lamport clock! (Make it make sense!)
If it caused it, it came before, and that’s all we need to know,
Lamport clock, Lamport clock, and the order’s set to go!

songs.note: Every member’s tape machine ran at a slightly different speed. The band stopped trying to agree on the time and agreed on the order instead.
songs.lesson: Machines in a distributed system have no single, perfectly shared clock. Lamport’s logical clocks (1978) order events by cause and effect instead, the “happened-before” relation: each process counts its own events, attaches the count to every message it sends, and when it receives a message jumps its count past the one it got. Anything that could have caused something else always gets a smaller timestamp.

songs.title: Slow or Dead

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I sent a message hours ago and nothing has come back,
Did it get lost? Is the server down? Did it fall right off the track?
Maybe it’s just slow, or maybe it’s already dead,
From here I cannot tell the difference, and that’s the dread!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Slow or dead? (I can’t tell!)
Slow or dead? (Ring the bell!)
In a distributed system some parts fail and some survive,
Slow or dead, slow or dead, is anybody alive?

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: One machine fails and the rest of them keep going,
Partial failure, and the others aren’t knowing.
Set a timeout, take a guess, and plan for being wrong,
The network isn’t reliable, it never was, so be strong!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: The network isn’t reliable! The latency’s not zero!
The topology will change, and there’s no single hero!

parts.label: Lead guitar break: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays a phrase and waits for the band to answer. Nothing. Four bars. Six. Just as Qword gives up and plays the next part alone, the answer arrives, late, right on top of it.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Slow or dead? (I can’t tell!)
Slow or dead? (Ring the bell!)
In a distributed system some parts fail and some survive,
Slow or dead, slow or dead, is anybody alive?

songs.note: In the snowstorm that split the tour, the two buses lost contact for two days. Each assumed the other had crashed. Neither had.
songs.lesson: In a distributed system, parts fail independently: one machine can crash while the rest keep running (partial failure). From the outside, a machine that’s slow looks exactly like one that’s dead, so systems use timeouts and have to cope with guessing wrong. The “fallacies of distributed computing” list the false assumptions that cause trouble, like “the network is reliable” and “latency is zero.”

songs.title: Consensus

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Five of us must agree on a single thing to do,
But messages get lost and some of us won’t make it through.
If a majority agrees, then the decision stands,
Even if two of us are silent, it’s still in our hands!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Consensus! (Agree!)
Consensus! (Majority!)
Three out of five and the choice is made for all,
Consensus, consensus, and the system will not fall!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Copy the data to many machines so one can fail and we survive,
But the copies have to agree, or the truth won’t stay alive.
Propose it, vote on it, and let a quorum decide,
Paxos and the leaders, and the log on every side!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Split brain! Two buses, two shows!
Nobody agreed, and now everybody knows!
An odd number of voters and a majority to win,
Count the duck as five and let the voting begin!

parts.label: Majority vote: full band
parts.desc: Each member proposes a different riff at the same time. Bar by bar, they listen and switch to whichever riff most of the band is playing, until three are playing the same one and the fourth falls in line.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Consensus! (Agree!)
Consensus! (Majority!)
Three out of five and the choice is made for all,
Consensus, consensus, and the system will not fall!

songs.note: With four members, every vote tied two to two, so they started counting Null as a fifth vote. The duck abstains every time.
songs.lesson: Consensus algorithms, like Paxos (1998), let a group of machines agree on a value even when some fail or messages get lost, usually by requiring a majority, called a quorum. With 2f + 1 machines, the group survives f failures. Replication keeps copies of data on several machines so one failure loses nothing. If a network split lets two groups each decide on their own, you get split brain.

songs.title: CAP

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The storm cut the line between the buses and the band,
Two halves that couldn’t talk, and a choice in each hand.
Keep on playing and risk that we don’t match,
Or stop until we’re back and leave the crowd with nothing to catch!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: C! (Everyone agrees!)
A! (Everyone gets an answer!)
P! (The network splits!)
And when it splits you choose: agree, or answer!
CAP! CAP! You can’t have it all,
Choose what matters when the partitions fall!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A bank will choose consistency, it stops instead of lying,
A shopping cart picks availability and keeps on trying.
Partitions will happen, so the real choice is clear,
Correct or always up, when the other side can’t hear!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Two buses! One city! Two shows, same night!
Both of them were available, and neither one was right!

parts.label: The partition: full band
parts.desc: The band splits in half, Nyble and Bytes on one side, Qword and Wyrd on the other, each half unable to hear the other. Both keep playing, and drift apart. When they can hear each other again, they stop, compare, and reconcile into one riff.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: C! (Everyone agrees!)
A! (Everyone gets an answer!)
P! (The network splits!)
And when it splits you choose: agree, or answer!
CAP! CAP! You can’t have it all,
Choose what matters when the partitions fall!

songs.note: The theorem was announced in 2000. The band read about it on the tour bus during the snowstorm and wrote this the same night.
songs.lesson: The CAP theorem (Eric Brewer, 2000, proved in 2002) says a distributed data store can’t guarantee all three of consistency (every node sees the same data), availability (every request gets an answer) and partition tolerance (it keeps working when the network splits). Network splits will happen, so during one, a system has to choose between staying consistent and staying available.

songs.title: Race Condition (Bytes First)

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Two of us reach for the same thing at the same time,
I read it, you read it, and we both think it’s fine.
I write it, you write it, and one of us is lost,
Whoever gets there last decides, and nobody counts the cost!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Race condition! (Who got there first?)
Race condition! (Better or worse?)
Same code, different timing, a different song each night,
Race condition, race condition, and nothing comes out right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It works on my machine, it works a thousand times,
Then once a week it fails and leaves no trace behind.
It hides when you go looking, it shows up when you’re gone,
The timing is the bug, and it’s been there all along!

parts.label: Bridge (rapped)
lines: Check, then act! You checked, it changed!
Read, modify, write, and the value’s rearranged!
Two threads, one variable, and nobody in charge,
Make it atomic, or the damage gets large!

parts.label: Turntable solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: The same two records, the same race. This time the right record wins by half a beat, the band follows the wrong one, and the song never recovers.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Race condition! (Who got there first?)
Race condition! (This time it’s worse!)
Same code, different timing, and the song falls apart tonight,
Race condition, race condition, and nothing comes out right!

songs.note: Hidden track. Version two of two. In this version, Bytes’s tape machine started first, the chorus came in a bar early, and the song never recovers.
songs.lesson: A race condition happens when a program’s result depends on the timing of things running at the same time. Two threads read the same value, both add one and both write it back, and one update is lost; or a thread checks something and it changes before it acts. Race conditions are intermittent and hard to reproduce: same program, same input, different result. The fix is to make the operation atomic or to synchronize access.
